care: If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

items.line: ‘In the beginning’: the start of everything, and how to read the six days. The readings Christians hold, and why these notes take no side on the age of the earth or on evolution.
‘Let Us make man in Our image’. Who is ‘Us’? The main readings, and what it means that male and female alike bear God's image.
A second account of creation, with a new name for God and a different order. How the two accounts relate, and the main views.
The woman's seed and the serpent's head: the ‘first gospel’ reading, the plainer reading, and how they fit together.
Where did Cain's wife come from? What the text says (5:4), and what it does not stop to explain.
The ‘sons of God’ and the daughters of men: angels, the line of Seth, or rulers. Three old readings, stated fairly.
‘The LORD regretted that He had made man’. Can God regret, when 1 Samuel 15:29 says he does not change his mind?
Noah's curse falls on Canaan, not Ham. The so-called ‘curse of Ham’, once used to defend the slavery of Africans, is a vile misuse of this text, named and rejected.
The tower of Babel: what the builders wanted, why God scattered them, and how Acts 2 answers the story.
Sodom, Lot's offer of his daughters and their later acts: what the text reports without approving, and how later Scripture names Sodom's sins.
God tells Abraham to offer his son. One of the hardest stories in the Bible, faced honestly.
The violence done to Dinah and her brothers' brutal revenge. A story Genesis tells without excusing anyone.
Judah and Tamar: a widow wronged, a trick, and a father-in-law who says, “She is more righteous than I”.
The midwives refuse Pharaoh's order and give him a false answer. How the text treats their deception, and how readers differ.
Moses kills an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew. Was it justice or murder? What the text says, and what it leaves open.
‘I AM WHO I AM’: what the name means, and how it is also a promise to be with his people.
‘I will harden his heart’: the three ways Exodus says it, and the Reformed and Arminian readings.
‘A bridegroom of blood’: one of the most obscure passages in the Old Testament, and the main readings.
God says he was not known to the patriarchs by his name the LORD. How this fits Genesis.
The death of the firstborn announced: judgment, grief, and how readers have faced it.
The night of the death of the firstborn, told soberly, with grief for Egypt's dead.
‘About 600,000 men on foot’: the readings of the Hebrew word for ‘thousand’.
The crossing of the sea: where it happened, and how readers understand it.
Manna and the Sabbath, and where Christians differ on keeping a Sabbath today.
The Ten Commandments: how Jewish, Catholic and Lutheran, and Reformed and Orthodox traditions number them.
‘Visiting the iniquity of the fathers’: what it means beside Ezekiel 18, and what it does not mean.
Laws about servants and slaves: what they were, how they differ from later slavery, and their misuse.
‘Eye for eye’ as a limit for judges, and the readings of the law on harm to a pregnant woman.
The Levites and the sword after the golden calf.
Why would God ask for animals to be killed and burned? What sacrifice meant in Leviticus, and what it did not mean.
Nadab and Abihu die for offering unauthorized fire. What the text says, what it leaves open, and the grief it does not hide.
The food laws: why some animals were unclean, and how Mark 7 and Acts 10 bear on Christians.
A mother is unclean after childbirth, and longer after a daughter. Uncleanness is not sin and not shame.
A person with a skin disease lives outside the camp. What the disease was, and what the chapter never says of the sick.
Bodily discharges and uncleanness: a status, not a verdict on any body or any woman.
The goat ‘for Azazel’: the main readings of an uncertain word.
How could a goat carry sins away? The Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur today, and how Hebrews reads it.
The life is in the blood: the ban on eating blood, and how Christians have understood it.
Child sacrifice to Molech, forbidden outright.
‘As with a woman’: the readings Christians hold, set out in their own terms. No one may use this verse to harm or shame any person.
The death penalties of chapter 20, stated soberly, and never as a pattern for today.
A priest with a physical defect may not serve at the altar. What the rule was, and why it says nothing of anyone's worth before God.
A man is put to death for cursing the Name, and ‘eye for eye’ as a limit on courts.
Slaves from other nations held for life: the passage faced honestly, with its misuse named.
The covenant curses: a warning to a nation, never God's verdict on one person's illness or loss.
Why are people given different values in silver? What the figures measured, and what they did not.
603,550 men of fighting age: the readings of the census totals, set out with no side taken.
The test for a wife suspected of adultery: what it permitted, what it restrained, and why it is no warrant for suspicion or control of any woman.
Quail, then a plague: the craving for Egypt and the judgment that followed.
Miriam is struck with a skin disease. Why this is never a statement about skin, race or illness.
Pardoned, and still barred from the land. Did Moses change God's mind?
A man is put to death for gathering sticks on the Sabbath. What the passage says and what it does not license.
Korah's revolt and the earth that opened: a judgment at Israel's beginning, and no weapon against a critic today.
Moses strikes the rock and is barred from the land. What was the fault?
A bronze snake on a pole, and how Jesus reads it in John 3:14-15.
The wars with Sihon and Og, and how Christians read the language of total destruction.
God tells Balaam to go and is then angry that he goes; and a donkey speaks.
A star from Jacob: how Jewish and Christian readers have understood Balaam's oracle.
Phinehas and the spear: why his zeal is no warrant for violence today.
A father or husband may cancel a woman's vow: a law of its world, not a rule for control today.
The command against Midian, the killing of captives and the keeping of the girls: one of the hardest chapters in the Bible, faced without softening.
Driving out the people of the land: read with the site's pages on the conquest, with no modern nation or conflict in view.
The cities of refuge, the avenger of blood, and the value the law sets on a human life.
The wars with Sihon and Og, and how Christians read the language of total destruction.
The Shema: what ‘the LORD is One’ means, its place in Jewish prayer, and how Christians confess the Trinity and keep it.
‘Devote them to complete destruction’: the readings Christians hold, and why no one may use the command to justify violence.
Israel chosen, and not for its size or its goodness: what being chosen means here and what it does not.
Death for the prophet, relative or town that leads Israel to other gods: a law of Israel's covenant, and no warrant for any church or state.
‘There will never cease to be poor in the land’: a reason to open the hand, never an excuse to close it.
The prophet like Moses: how Jewish and Christian readers have understood the promise.
The rules of war and the cities of Canaan, read with the site's pages on the conquest.
The woman captured in war: what the law restrained and what it still allowed, faced without defending it.
The stubborn and rebellious son: what the law says, and why it gives no parent a right to harm a child.
‘Anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse’, and how Paul reads it in Galatians 3:13.
The laws on rape and seduction, among the hardest in the law. Nothing here asks any victim to marry or stay with anyone.
Who may enter the assembly, read beside Ruth the Moabite and Isaiah 56.
The certificate of divorce, and what Jesus says about it in Matthew 19.
‘Blot out the memory of Amalek’: a command about one ancient people, with no people of today in view.
The curses: addressed to a nation in covenant, never God's verdict on a person's illness or loss, and never a judgment on the Jewish people's later sufferings.
‘The word is very near you’: what Moses meant, and how Paul uses it in Romans 10.
Moses is forbidden the land. Why, and what his death in sight of it means.
Who wrote of the death of Moses? What the last chapter shows about how the book was finished.
Rahab hides the scouts and lies to the king's men: how readers have weighed her lie, and what the New Testament praises her for.
The Jordan stops flowing: the ways readers have understood the crossing.
The commander of the LORD's army and his answer, ‘Neither’: who he is, and what the answer means.
Jericho ‘devoted to destruction’: the readings Christians hold, and why no one may use the chapter to justify violence.
Achan and his household: how readers have understood the deaths of his sons and daughters.
The altar on Mount Ebal: why the ceremony stands here in the book, far north of Ai.
The oath to Gibeon: why a promise won by a trick still bound Israel.
The sun stands still: the ways the words are read.
‘Leaving no survivors’: the sweeping summaries, and the survivors the book itself reports.
‘It was of the LORD to harden their hearts’: how readers have understood the hardening.
‘Very much of the land remains’: how complete the conquest was.
The cities of refuge: a hearing set between a death and revenge.
The altar by the Jordan: zeal, suspicion, and a war avoided by asking first.
The warning against marriage with the nations: a matter of worship and not of birth.
‘Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve’: a call set inside a covenant God had already made.
‘You are not able to serve the LORD’: why Joshua answers the people's promise this way.
Adoni-bezek's thumbs and big toes: the cruelty of the age, and the captured king's own verdict on it.
The LORD was with Judah, yet the iron chariots stayed: two ways of reading the chapter's failures.
Why the nations were left in the land: judgment, and a test.
Ehud and Eglon: an assassination by a trick, and how readers have weighed the means.
Jael and Sisera: a guest's trust broken, and how readers have weighed her act.
The song's praise of Jael, and Sisera's mother at the window.
The fleece: a way to seek guidance, or weak faith met by God's patience?
Gideon's revenge on Succoth and Penuel: a deliverer turning on his own people.
Gideon refuses the crown, then makes an ephod that becomes a snare.
Abimelech murders his seventy brothers to make himself king.
God sends a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and Shechem: what the words mean.
Jephthah's vow and his daughter: the two main readings, and why nothing here praises the vow.
Shibboleth: men of Israel killed at the fords for the way they spoke.
‘This was from the LORD’: God at work through Samson's wrong choices.
Samson's death: the ways readers have understood his last act and his prayer.
The Danites destroy a tranquil town: the forms of conquest without God's word.
The Levite's concubine: what was done to her, and why no reading may excuse the men or blame her.
Israel asks God about a war on Benjamin, and loses twice: a war among brothers.
The young women of Jabesh-gilead and Shiloh, taken without being asked, and the book's last verdict.
Famine, Moab and three deaths: whether the family's choices brought judgment, and why the text leaves it open.
Ruth's vow to Naomi: what it bound her to, and why it is more than a wedding reading.
Naomi calls herself Mara and says the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her: a complaint the book does not rebuke.
‘She happened to come’: chance, and the quiet hand of God.
Naomi's plan: bold, risky, and how readers have judged it.
The night at the threshing floor: what happened, and the two ways readers have read it.
‘You must also acquire the widow’: the language of buying, and why it does not make Ruth property.
A Moabite in Israel when Deuteronomy 23:3 shuts Moab out: the answers readers have given.
Ten names from Perez to David: a family line that chooses its names.
‘The LORD had closed her womb’: what the words say about God, and what they do not say about anyone who has no children.
Hannah gives her young son to serve at Shiloh: what her vow meant, and how readers have weighed it.
Eli's sons abuse their office and the women at the tent, and their father does not stop them.
Why the guilt of Eli's house could not be wiped away by sacrifice or offering.
Why God let the ark be captured: the sign of his presence is not a charm.
The men of Beth-shemesh struck down for looking into the ark.
Why asking for a king is called a rejection of God, when the law allowed for one.
Saul's offering at Gilgal: why an offering made too soon cost Saul a lasting kingdom.
Saul's rash oath, the lot that fell on Jonathan, and the people who saved him.
The command to destroy the Amalekites, children and infants included: how Christians read it, and what no one may do with it.
The LORD regretted making Saul king, yet does not change his mind: two truths held together.
‘A spirit of distress from the LORD’: what the words mean, and why the text names no illness.
Jonathan's love for David: what the text says, and how readers have understood it.
Michal and the bride-price: a daughter's love turned into a plot against David.
Michal's lie, and a household idol in David's house: told, not approved.
David and the holy bread, and why Mark 2:26 names Abiathar.
The massacre of the priests of Nob, and David's ‘I myself am responsible’.
‘The LORD’s anointed’: why David spared Saul, and why the chapter gives no shield to leaders who do wrong.
David's oath to kill every male of Nabal's house, and the woman who turned him back.
David's raids from Ziklag, and the lies he told Achish: reported, not approved.
The medium at Endor: did Samuel really appear, and what the chapter says about seeking the dead.
Saul's death by his own hand: told with sorrow, and never as a way out.
The Amalekite's story of Saul's death, which does not match 1 Samuel 31, and why David had him put to death.
David's words for Jonathan, ‘surpassing the love of women’: what they say, and how readers have understood them.
A contest at the pool of Gibeon, and a war of brother against brother.
Joab murders Abner, and David curses him but does not punish him.
The murder of Ish-bosheth, and the harsh punishment of the men who killed him.
‘The blind and the lame’: a hard saying at the taking of Jerusalem, and what it does not mean.
Why Uzzah died when he took hold of the ark.
‘I will be his Father, and he will be My son’: Solomon first, and how the New Testament reads the promise.
A throne forever, and the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC: did the promise fail?
David's harsh treatment of the Moabite prisoners, told without praise or blame.
David takes Bathsheba: the king's power, and why the text lays the guilt on him.
The letter that sent Uriah to his death.
Why the child born to Bathsheba died, and David's words, ‘I will go to him’.
The rape of Tamar, the silence pressed on her, and a father who did nothing.
Was David right to bring Absalom home without justice or repentance?
‘The LORD has told him so’: David and Shimei's curses.
Absalom and his father's concubines: ten women used as a sign of power.
Joab kills Absalom against the king's command.
Ziba or Mephibosheth: who told David the truth?
Joab murders Amasa on the road, and goes unpunished in David's lifetime.
Seven of Saul's descendants put to death for Saul's crime, and Rizpah's vigil.
Elhanan and ‘the brother of Goliath’: a verse that differs from 1 Chronicles 20:5.
How David could call himself blameless after Bathsheba and Uriah.
The LORD stirred up David to take a census, and 1 Chronicles names Satan.
Seventy thousand die for the king's sin: ‘these sheep, what have they done?’
Abishag, a young woman brought to an old king's bed, who is never asked and never speaks.
Did David really promise Solomon the throne, or did a prophet and a mother press it on an old man?
Adonijah put to death for asking to marry Abishag.
Joab killed at the altar, and a kingdom established by executions: justice or ruthless politics?
Pharaoh's daughter and the high places: a quiet warning at the start of Solomon's reign.
‘Cut the living child in two’: the sword that found the true mother.
Forty thousand stalls or four thousand: where the BSB follows Chronicles.
Four hundred and eighty years after the exodus: what the number means for dating the exodus.
Ten cubits across and thirty around: does the bronze Sea make pi equal three?
If heaven cannot contain God, why build him a house?
Twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep: are the numbers literal?
Canaanite slave labor, and an Israelite levy that the north called a heavy yoke.
Gold, horses from Egypt and silver like stones: praise, or a quiet charge under Deuteronomy 17?
Seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and a heart turned to other gods.
‘This turn of events was from the LORD’: God's purpose and Rehoboam's folly.
Jeroboam's golden calves: images of other gods, or pedestals for the LORD?
Why the man of God died for being deceived while the old prophet who lied lived.
Why the one good child in Jeroboam's house died.
Asa, whose heart was devoted to the LORD, pays the king of Aram to attack Israel.
Baasha condemned for destroying Jeroboam's house, though God had said it would happen.
Hiel rebuilds Jericho at the cost of two of his sons.
Why would God let the son of the widow who sheltered his prophet die?
The prophets of Baal killed at the Kishon, and why it gives no one a warrant for violence today.
Elijah asks to die under a broom tree, and how God answers him.
A man killed by a lion, and Ahab condemned for sparing the king of Aram.
Naboth condemned by false witnesses under the forms of the law.
Judgment delayed to Ahab's son: is it fair?
A lying spirit in the mouths of the prophets: does God deceive?
Fire on two captains and their fifty men, who came on their king's orders.
Elisha curses a jeering crowd at Bethel, and two bears maul forty-two of them.
Mesha sacrifices his son on the wall, and great fury falls on Israel: whose fury?
A creditor coming to take a widow's two children as slaves.
A mother's only son dies in her lap, and she goes to the prophet.
Naaman asks pardon in advance for bowing in the temple of Rimmon, and Elisha says, Go in peace.
Gehazi's greed, and Naaman's disease on him and his descendants.
Famine in besieged Samaria, and a king who blames God.
The officer who scoffed is trampled to death in the gate.
Did Elisha tell Hazael to lie to the king, or encourage him to murder?
Jehu kills Joram on Naboth's land and has Ahaziah of Judah shot.
Jezebel thrown from a window, as Elijah had said.
Ahab's seventy sons killed at Jehu's command.
God praises Jehu's purge, and Hosea later condemns the blood of Jezreel.
Athaliah sets out to destroy the royal family, and a baby is hidden.
Kings speaks well of Joash, and Chronicles tells of his turning and a prophet stoned.
Elisha angry at a king who struck the ground three times.
A dead man revived at the touch of Elisha's bones.
Jeroboam II did evil, and Israel prospered under him.
Menahem's atrocity at Tiphsah, reported without comment.
Ahaz sacrifices his son in the fire.
The fall of Samaria explained as judgment.
The settlers in Samaria, and the Samaritans' own story.
Hezekiah, who trusted the LORD, pays tribute and strips the temple doors.
The Assyrian camp struck in one night.
Hezekiah hears of exile to come and thinks of peace in his own lifetime.
Manasseh's child sacrifice and the innocent blood that filled Jerusalem.
Huldah promised Josiah a peaceful grave, and he died in battle.
Josiah kills the priests of the high places on their altars.
‘The LORD was unwilling to forgive’: what that means.
Zedekiah's sons killed before his eyes.
If God chose Jerusalem, how could he let the city and the temple burn?
Why would a history begin with nine chapters of names?
Was David the seventh son of Jesse, as here, or the eighth, as 1 Samuel says?
Who was Zerubbabel's father, Pedaiah or Shealtiel?
Is the prayer of Jabez a formula for success?
The huge numbers of warriors, animals and captives.
Was Samuel a Levite or an Ephraimite?
Why are Dan and Zebulun missing from the genealogies?
Names with Baal in Saul's family, changed in Samuel.
Why the list of Jerusalem's residents differs from Nehemiah 11.
Saul's death on Mount Gilboa.
Saul ‘failed to inquire of the LORD’, though 1 Samuel 28:6 says he did.
Why Chronicles leaves out David's years over Judah alone and the civil war.
The troop numbers, and why Judah's is so small.
Why God struck Uzzah dead when he tried to keep the ark from falling.
Does the chapter blame Uzzah, or David?
Why the Bible celebrates David's wars.
Who killed Goliath: David, or Elhanan? And where is Bathsheba?
Who incited the census: God (2 Samuel 24:1) or Satan?
Different numbers from 2 Samuel 24 for the census and the price.
Seventy thousand dead in a plague for the king's sin.
Why David, whose victories God gave, could not build the temple.
Why Asahel is listed as a commander after his death.
Can the enormous amounts of gold and silver be historical?
Solomon's horses and chariots, which the law warned kings against.
The foreigners Solomon put to forced labor.
If heaven cannot contain God, what did the temple mean?
Is 7:14 a promise to a modern nation?
God's warning that he would uproot Israel and reject the temple.
‘This turn of events was from God’: did God cause the division?
Humbled and spared, but still made Shishak's servants.
Armies of 400,000 and 800,000, and 500,000 slain.
Did Asa remove the high places or not?
Asa ‘did not seek the LORD, but only the physicians’.
A lying spirit sent by the LORD to Ahab's prophets.
The enemy armies destroy one another.
Jehoram's illness, foretold in a letter from Elijah.
Athaliah's attempt to destroy the royal family.
Zechariah's murder, and why Matthew 23:35 calls him the son of Berechiah.
Ten thousand thrown from a cliff.
Uzziah struck with a skin disease for burning incense.
Ahaz sacrificed his sons in the fire.
Passover eaten by people not ritually clean, and God heals them.
‘God left him alone to test him’.
Manasseh's child sacrifice and sorcery.
Manasseh's repentance, which Kings does not tell.
Josiah killed for not heeding ‘God’ speaking through Pharaoh Neco.
If God chose Jerusalem, how could he let the city and the temple burn?
A Persian king who speaks of the LORD as the God who appointed him to build a temple, and what the Cyrus Cylinder shows.
The vessels counted out add up to 2,499, and the total given is 5,400.
The list of those who came home: its figures add up to less than its total, and differ from the copy in Nehemiah 7.
Families and priests who could not prove their descent, and a question left open for God to settle.
Shouts of joy and loud weeping at the new foundation, and no one could tell them apart.
Who laid the foundation: Zerubbabel and Jeshua (3:8-10), Sheshbazzar (5:16), or the builders of 520 BC (Haggai 2:18)?
Help refused from neighbors who said they worshiped the same God.
A leap forward in time to Xerxes and Artaxerxes, and a letter that stopped the rebuilding of the city.
Darius's threat against anyone who interferes: a Persian king's decree, recorded and not commanded by God.
When Ezra came: 458, 428 or 398 BC, and whether he came before Nehemiah or after.
A foreign king's letter gives Ezra power to enforce God's law with heavy penalties.
Ezra will not ask for soldiers to guard the road, though Nehemiah later travels with them.
‘The holy seed has been mixed’: a line drawn by faith, by birth, or both?
A prayer that confesses the people's guilt as the speaker's own and asks for nothing.
A covenant to send away foreign wives and their children: what the text says, how readers weigh it, and why it gives no one today a warrant to break up a family.
Four men who opposed the plan, or who oversaw it: the Hebrew can be read both ways.
The book ends with a list of names, and with a last verse whose Hebrew is hard to read.
Chislev before Nisan in the same twentieth year: how the king's years were counted.
Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem: who they were, and why a walled Jerusalem threatened them.
The builders of the wall, and the nobles of Tekoa who would not put their shoulders to the work.
Nehemiah prays that his enemies' sin not be blotted out: a cry for justice handed to God.
Building with one hand and holding a weapon with the other: armed only for defense.
Families forced to sell their children into slavery to their own people, and why the law allowed debt service at all.
A hired prophet, and how Nehemiah knew that God had not sent him.
The list of the first returnees again: its figures differ from Ezra 2 and fall short of the total.
‘Explaining it and giving insight’: reading clearly, or translating into Aramaic?
No such Feast of Tabernacles since Joshua's day, though the Bible records earlier ones.
The ordinances ‘by which a man will live if he practices them’, and how Paul reads the same words.
A pledge that differs in places from the law of Moses: a third of a shekel, wood by lot, no Sabbath trade.
Lists that run to Jaddua and a later Darius: who wrote them, and when.
The law excluding Ammonites and Moabites read aloud, and Ruth the Moabite in David's line.
Nehemiah beats men and pulls out their hair: told without comment, and no warrant for harming anyone today.
A book that ends not in triumph but with a prayer to be remembered.
Is Esther history? Greek sources name Xerxes' queen as Amestris, not Vashti or Esther.
Vashti refuses to be put on show before drunken guests, and loses her crown: defiance, or a right refusal?
Young women taken into the king's harem without their consent, and Esther among them.
Esther hides her people at Mordecai's command: prudence, or compromise?
Mordecai's family was carried into exile in 597 BC, more than a century before: whom does the verse mean?
Why Mordecai would not bow to Haman, when Israelites bowed to kings and officials elsewhere.
A decree to destroy a whole people on one day, and how the book holds that hatred up to be seen.
The book's turning point names neither God nor prayer: relief ‘from another place’.
‘And if I perish, I perish’: Esther goes to the king against the law.
A gallows fifty cubits high, and what the word for it means.
A sleepless king and a record read at the right page: providence, or coincidence?
Esther is silent as Haman begs for his life: is she cruel?
Does Mordecai's decree permit the killing of women and children? The Hebrew can be read two ways.
The fighting of the thirteenth of Adar: how readers weigh it, and why it gives no one a warrant to harm anyone.
Esther asks for a second day in Susa.
Purim, a feast the law of Moses did not command, kept to this day.
Who is the accuser? Some see a member of the heavenly court with the role of prosecutor; most Christian readers identify him with Satan.
Job's ten children die in one day. The book tells it in two verses and does not explain it to Job.
Job worships in grief, and the next chapter shows that worship and anguish can stand together.
Is Job's wife wicked, or a grieving mother? She has lost the same ten children.
Job curses the day of his birth and longs for death. The book does not scold him for it.
Eliphaz says many true things. Why does God later say the friends did not speak rightly?
No mediator between Job and God: Job's first longing for someone to stand between them.
‘Though He slay me, I will hope in Him’: faith and protest in one verse.
Who is Job's Redeemer, and does he expect to see God after death? Both are debated.
Eliphaz charges Job with crimes he never committed, because his theology needs them.
Who speaks the poem on wisdom, and why does it stand here?
Is Elihu a wise voice or another failed comforter? The text does not settle it.
Why does God not explain Job's suffering? What the speeches answer, and what they do not.
Behemoth: the hippopotamus, a mythic beast, or both described in heightened language?
Leviathan: the crocodile, the chaos monster, or a real creature in the language of chaos?
Does the happy ending undo the book's message? New children do not replace the ones Job lost.
‘Kiss the Son’: the Hebrew is hard to read, and Bibles render it in different ways. What the choices are, and why.
‘Who can praise You from Sheol?’ What the psalmists knew, and did not yet know, of life after death.
‘According to my righteousness’: is the psalmist claiming to be sinless? Innocence of a false charge, not perfection.
‘A little lower than the angels’, or ‘than God’? The Hebrew word, the Greek, and how Hebrews reads it.
‘There is no God’ in the wicked man's schemes: practical godlessness, not a philosopher's doubt.
‘My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?’ The psalm Jesus prayed on the cross, and the ways it is read.
A whole people says it kept faith and suffered anyway. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 8:36.
‘Brought forth in iniquity’: what this says about sin from birth, and what it does not say about a mother.
‘Wash their feet in the blood of the wicked’: one of the cursing psalms, and how Christians read it.
‘You are gods’: who is being spoken to, and why Jesus quotes the line in John 10:34.
The one lament that never turns, ending ‘darkness is my closest companion’. Why God kept it.
‘May his children be fatherless’: one of the cursing psalms. Acts 1:20 applies the verse before it to Judas.
‘The LORD said to my Lord’: the verse the New Testament uses most, and how Jews and Christians read it.
The hardest line in the Psalms. The main Christian readings, side by side, and why none of them permits harm.
Wisdom laughs at the calamity of those who refused her. A prophet's warning in poetry, spoken while there is still time to turn.
Long life and full barns for those who trust the LORD: the usual fruit of wisdom, not a guarantee against loss.
The forbidden woman. The warning is written to a son, but the danger it names belongs to both sexes, and the book teaches no contempt for women.
Getting free from a pledge for another's debt: wise caution about rash promises, not a ban on helping anyone.
‘The LORD created me’. Poetry about God's wisdom, and a battleground in the fourth century over whether the Son was created.
Idle hands make one poor. A pattern for the reader's own habits, never a verdict that the poor deserve their poverty (13:23).
The rod and the son. Faithful parents read it in two ways; neither reading gives anyone a warrant to harm a child.
The LORD made even the wicked for the day of disaster: nothing escapes his purpose, not that he creates anyone in order to destroy them.
A bribe works like a charm in the eyes of the one who gives it. An observation, condemned elsewhere in the book (17:23).
A quarrelsome wife. A picture of a home full of strife, not a license to despise anyone or a reason to stay in danger.
Train up a child. How things usually go, not a promise that blames parents whose grown children walk away.
Strike him with a rod. Read with 13:24: correction instead of neglect, in readings that differ, and never a warrant for harm.
Do not answer a fool, and answer a fool: two true sayings set side by side, and wisdom knows which one the moment needs.
Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint. Vision here is God's word to his people, not a plan for the future.
What is the name of his Son? Read as Israel, as an ironic challenge, or as a glimpse that later Scripture takes up.
The woman of noble character: praise, not a standard every woman must meet. Its heart is the fear of the LORD (31:30).
Matthew and Luke give Jesus two different family trees, with different fathers for Joseph. How do they fit?
Isaiah's Hebrew says a young woman; the Greek Matthew quotes says a virgin. What did Isaiah mean, and what does Matthew claim?
Herod kills the little boys of Bethlehem. No other ancient writer records it. What can be known, and how do we read such grief?
‘He will be called a Nazarene’ is not found in any Old Testament book. What is Matthew quoting?
Jesus says he came to fulfil the Law, not abolish it. Then why do Christians not keep all of it?
Tear out your eye? How to read Jesus' strongest picture-language without hurting yourself or others.
Only Matthew has the words ‘except for sexual immorality’. Christians read this exception in several ways.
Jesus sends the Twelve only to Israel, yet the book ends with all nations. Why the change?
Jesus seems to call a Canaanite mother a dog. What is happening in this hard exchange?
Who or what is the rock? Peter himself, his confession of faith, or Christ? Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers answer differently.
Some standing here will not die before they see the Son of Man coming. Did that happen?
The woes against scribes and Pharisees are a warning to religious leaders, never a verdict on the Jewish people. That misuse is named and rejected.
‘This generation will not pass away.’ Is Jesus speaking of the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, of his return, or of both?
Eternal punishment and eternal life: what the sheep and the goats teach about judgment.
‘His blood be on us.’ For centuries this cry was misused to blame all Jews. That reading is wrong; here is why.
Only Matthew says that tombs opened and saints were raised when Jesus died. How have readers taken it?
Mark names Isaiah, but the first words come from Malachi and Exodus. Why?
Was Jesus moved by compassion or by anger when he touched the leper? The manuscripts differ.
Jesus names Abiathar as high priest, but 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech.
Jesus' own family thinks he is out of his mind.
What is the sin that will never be forgiven?
Does Jesus tell parables so that outsiders will not understand?
“Thus all foods are clean”: did Jesus set aside the food laws?
Some standing here will see the kingdom come with power. Did that happen?
Why does Jesus curse a fig tree when it was not the season for figs?
“This generation will not pass away”: was Jesus wrong about the end?
How can the Son not know the day or the hour?
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” Was Jesus abandoned by God?
Does Mark really end with frightened women saying nothing?
The census ‘while Quirinius was governor of Syria’. A real historical difficulty, the main explanations, and why the notes take no side.
Jesus reminds his home town that Elijah and Elisha were sent to outsiders, and they try to kill him. Why did that make them so angry?
‘Blessed are you who are poor’ and ‘woe to you who are rich’. Does Luke mean money, or the heart? Both, and how they fit.
‘I have come to ignite a fire on the earth’ and to bring division. How does that fit the Prince of Peace?
Hate your father and mother? What the word meant in Jesus' way of speaking, and what it still demands.
The master praises a dishonest manager. What is being praised, and what is not?
The rich man and Lazarus. Is this a picture of the life to come, a parable about wealth, or both?
Is the kingdom of God ‘within you’ or ‘in your midst’? What the Greek allows.
‘Buy a sword’, and then ‘That is enough’. Was Jesus arming his disciples?
The angel and the sweat like drops of blood. Missing from some of the oldest copies; what that means.
‘Father, forgive them’. A prayer missing from some early copies, and why scholars are divided.
‘Today you will be with Me in Paradise’. What did Jesus promise the dying thief?
‘The Word was God’, or ‘a god’, as one translation has it? What the Greek says, explained in plain words.
Is Jesus rude to his mother when he calls her ‘Woman’? What the word meant then.
‘Born of water and the Spirit’: is the water baptism, natural birth, or the cleansing God promised in Ezekiel 36? Christians differ.
‘Eat the flesh and drink the blood’: is Jesus speaking of the Lord's Supper, of believing in him, or both? Churches read it differently.
The woman caught in adultery: is it part of John? What the old copies show, and why Bibles keep it.
‘You belong to your father, the devil’: hard words to particular opponents in a bitter argument. Never a word against the Jewish people.
‘Before Abraham was born, I am’: why his hearers picked up stones, and what ‘I am’ may echo.
‘I and the Father are one’: one in purpose, or one in being? How the church came to read it.
‘No one comes to the Father except through Me’: what it claims, and what Christians say about those who never heard.
‘The Father is greater than I’: does this make the Son less than God? How the creeds answer.
Forgiving sins and withholding forgiveness: what did Jesus give the disciples? Churches answer in different ways.
Thomas calls Jesus ‘my Lord and my God’, and Jesus accepts it. What a Jew meant by those words.
Who are the ‘we’ who vouch for the disciple's witness, and what does it say about who wrote the book?
How did Judas die? Matthew says he hanged himself; Acts says he fell and burst open. The difference, faced honestly, and the ways readers answer it.
Tongues at Pentecost: known languages, heard by people from many lands. And how Christians differ on the gift of tongues today.
‘Whom you crucified’. Said by a Jew to his own people, with forgiveness offered. Why this verse may never be turned against the Jewish people.
‘Repent and be baptized’ for ‘the forgiveness of your sins’. How the churches read baptism, forgiveness and ‘your children’.
‘Everything in common’. What the first believers did, freely, and why it is not a program for any modern economy.
‘No other name’. What the text claims about Jesus, and where Christians differ about those who never heard.
Ananias and Sapphira. A hard story, not softened: what their sin was, and how readers have understood the judgment.
Gamaliel's Theudas, and the Theudas of Josephus who seems to come later. The problem stated honestly, and the answers given.
Stephen places Abraham's purchase at Shechem; Genesis puts it at Hebron. How readers account for the difference.
Believers in Samaria baptized, yet without the Spirit until the apostles came. One time, or a pattern?
Did Paul's companions hear the voice (9:7) or not understand it (22:9)? What the Greek allows.
The council's four rules for Gentile believers. Food laws, or something else? And do they still bind?
The salvation of God ‘sent to the Gentiles’. Does Acts end by closing the door to the Jews? Two readings.
‘The wrath of God’. What Paul means by it, said plainly: God handing people over to what they have chosen. And what can be known of God from the world he made.
Same-sex relations in 1:26-27. What Paul says, how Christians read it, and why the very next verse turns the charge on anyone who judges.
Gentiles who ‘do by nature what the law requires’. Who are they, and what does it say about those who never heard?
‘The atoning sacrifice’. Propitiation, expiation or mercy seat, and how Christians understand what the cross did.
Sin and death through one man. Original sin in the Western and Eastern churches, a question of translation, and Adam and human origins.
‘I do not do what I want to do’. Is the ‘I’ a believer, a person before faith, or Israel or Adam speaking? Three readings.
‘All things work together for good’. What the verse promises and what it does not, and how churches read ‘predestined’.
‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’. What the words meant in Malachi, and whether Paul speaks of persons or of peoples.
God has mercy on whom he wants, and hardens whom he wants. The potter and the clay, and how Reformed and Arminian readers take it.
‘And so all Israel will be saved’. Who is ‘all Israel’, and when? The main readings, with no claim about any modern state.
‘Submit to the governing authorities’. What it asks, what it does not, and how Christians have read it under unjust rulers.
Andronicus and Junia, ‘outstanding among the apostles’. Junia as a woman, and what the phrase and the word ‘apostle’ may mean.
‘Christ did not send me to baptize’. What Paul means about baptism, and why it does not make baptism unimportant.
‘Saved, but only as if through the flames’. How Catholics and Protestants each read the testing fire.
‘Hand this man over to Satan’. What it most likely means, how churches practise discipline, and how it must never be used.
The list of those who will not inherit the kingdom, and the two Greek words joined in one phrase. What Paul says, how Christians read it, and ‘that is what some of you were’.
Divorce and remarriage: what Jesus said, what Paul adds, and how churches read ‘not bound’. Nothing here asks anyone to stay in danger.
A word to slaves that can be translated two ways, set beside ‘do not become slaves of men’.
‘An idol is nothing’, and one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ: Jesus inside Israel's confession of the one God.
Head coverings in worship: what Paul asks, what it meant in Corinth, and how churches read it today.
Eating ‘in an unworthy manner’, and why some were sick. What Paul means by recognizing the body.
‘Women are to be silent in the churches’. The puzzle of these verses beside 11:5, and the views.
‘Baptized for the dead’. One of the most puzzling verses in the Bible, and why its meaning is uncertain.
A curse and a prayer in one verse: ‘Come, O Lord’, an Aramaic prayer left untranslated in a Greek letter.
‘We despaired even of life.’ Paul says he was given more than he could bear. What that means beside 1 Corinthians 10:13, and why no one should carry such a weight alone.
Forgive and comfort the man who was punished. Who he may have been, why discipline aims at restoring a person, and why forgiving is not the same as putting others back in danger.
‘The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.’ What Paul means by the letter, and why it is not a rule about reading the Bible loosely.
The veil over Moses' face and over hearts. Why this is not contempt for the law or for the Jewish people, and why the long misuse of these verses must be rejected.
The earthly tent and the heavenly house. What happens to a believer who dies, and how Christians read ‘at home with the Lord’.
‘God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf.’ Sin or sin offering, and how different traditions describe the great exchange.
‘Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers.’ What the yoke picture means, what Paul had in view in Corinth, and why it is no reason to leave a husband or wife.
‘Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor.’ Why Paul's appeal for money rests on the story of Christ, and what it does not promise.
‘False apostles.’ Who Paul's rivals may have been, and why his quarrel with them is about a way of ministry, not about who they were by birth.
A man caught up to the third heaven and to Paradise. Why Paul speaks of himself as ‘a man in Christ’, and why he will not say more.
The thorn in the flesh. What it may have been, why no one knows, and the answer Paul was given instead of healing.
‘Examine yourselves.’ Why this verse was not written to make anxious believers doubt without end.
‘Let him be under a curse.’ Why Paul speaks so fiercely about another gospel, and why this gives no one licence to curse those they disagree with.
Paul opposes Peter at Antioch. What Peter did, why Paul said it to his face, and why the story is told without contempt for Peter.
‘Not by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ.’ The two readings of ‘works of the law’, and ‘faith in’ or ‘faithfulness of’ Christ.
‘Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.’ What the curse was, and what the cross did.
‘Seed’, not ‘seeds’. How Paul reads the promise to Abraham as pointing to Christ.
‘All of you who were baptized into Christ.’ What churches agree on about baptism, and where they differ.
‘Neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.’ What all agree it says about standing in Christ, and where churches differ on what follows.
Hagar and Sarah. What Paul's picture means, why it is no verdict on Hagar or on the Jewish people, and the misuse that must be rejected.
‘You have fallen away from grace.’ What Paul warns against, and how Christians read it alongside God's promise to keep his people.
Paul's harshest sentence. Why he wrote it, and why it is not a pattern for how believers speak.
‘The Israel of God.’ Whether Paul means the whole church, Jewish believers in Jesus, or Israel as a people.
‘To the saints in Ephesus.’ Why some early copies leave out ‘in Ephesus’, and what that may say about the letter.
Chosen and predestined in Christ. How Reformed and Arminian or Wesleyan Christians read these words, and why they are written as praise.
‘By grace you have been saved through faith … not by works.’ Grace, faith and the good works God prepared.
The dividing wall torn down. What wall, what ‘abolishing’ the law means, and why it is no word against the Jewish people.
‘He also descended to the lower parts of the earth.’ The incarnation, the grave, or the realm of the dead.
Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers. Whether some of these gifts have ceased, and how churches differ.
‘Be angry, yet do not sin.’ What to do with anger, and what this verse does not ask of someone who has been wronged.
Wives and husbands. What all agree on, the complementarian and egalitarian readings, and why this passage never tells anyone to stay in danger.
Slaves and masters. What the text said to its first hearers, how it was misused to defend slavery, and why that was wrong.
The armour of God. A struggle not against flesh and blood, and why it is no licence for aggression toward anyone.
‘Overseers and deacons.’ What these leaders were, and why churches today read them differently.
‘To depart and be with Christ.’ What all Christians confess about death, and where they differ about the time before the resurrection.
‘He emptied Himself.’ Why this never meant Christ stopped being God, as the creeds confess.
‘Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.’ Not earning it: God's work and ours together.
‘Those dogs … those mutilators of the flesh.’ Whom Paul meant, and why this is no word against the Jewish people.
Faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? Two readings of one Greek phrase.
‘Be anxious for nothing.’ An invitation to prayer, not a rebuke of anxious people.
‘I can do all things.’ Contentment in hunger and in plenty, not a slogan for ambition.
‘My God will supply all your needs.’ Why this is not a promise of wealth.
‘The firstborn over all creation.’ Why this does not make the Son a created being, as the creeds confess.
‘If indeed you continue in your faith.’ Holding on, and what Christians say about assurance.
‘What is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions.’ Why this is no lack in the cross.
The teaching that troubled the church: what the letter shows, and why Paul answers with Christ.
Food, feasts and Sabbaths, ‘a shadow of the things to come’. How Christians keep, or do not keep, a day.
Wives and husbands. What all agree on, the two readings, and why this passage never tells anyone to stay in danger.
Slaves and masters. What the text said to its first hearers, how it was misused to defend slavery, and why that was wrong.
‘Gentle among you’, or ‘infants among you’? One letter in Greek, and why both readings say the same thing about Paul.
Paul's hard words about those who opposed the gospel in Judea. Why they are no verdict on the Jewish people, then or now.
‘Satan obstructed us.’ What Paul meant, and what he did next.
‘God’s will that you should be holy.’ Sexual holiness, stated plainly and without contempt for any person.
‘Caught up … to meet the Lord in the air.’ What all Christians confess, and the main readings of the rapture and the return.
‘We who are alive and remain.’ Did Paul expect to be alive when the Lord came?
‘Like a thief in the night.’ Why the Day of the Lord comes with no date attached.
‘Spirit, soul, and body.’ Three parts of a person, or the whole person?
‘Eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord.’ What all Christians confess about judgment, and where they differ.
‘The Day of the Lord has already come.’ What frightened the church, and why Paul said not yet.
‘The man of lawlessness.’ The main readings through history, why none is certain, and why no living person should be named.
‘What is now restraining him.’ The Thessalonians knew; the main suggestions since.
‘God will send them a powerful delusion.’ God giving people over to the lie they chose.
‘Keep away from any brother.’ Discipline that still treats a person as family.
‘If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.’ Said of those who refused, never a word against the poor or those who cannot work.
The list of lawbreakers, and the word the BSB renders ‘homosexuals’. Both readings, and three things that are plain on either.
‘Handed over to Satan.’ Church discipline meant to correct, and never to silence the harmed.
‘For kings and all those in authority.’ Prayer for every ruler, and no party lesson.
‘I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority.’ What all agree, and the complementarian and egalitarian readings.
‘Saved through childbearing.’ The main readings, and why no woman's worth depends on bearing children.
‘The husband of but one wife.’ Four readings of one phrase.
‘The women.’ Deacons' wives, or women deacons?
‘The Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe.’ What the verse says, and does not say.
Accusations against elders: fairness to the accused, and never a way to silence a report of abuse.
‘Use a little wine.’ Abstinence and moderation, each fairly.
Slaves and masters. Why Paul did not command the end of slavery, and the misuse of these verses.
‘The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil.’ Not money itself, and not a promise of wealth.
‘Who has abolished death.’ What it means when believers still die.
Onesiphorus: was he dead, and is Paul praying for him? Two readings.
‘If we deny Him, He will also deny us’, and ‘He remains faithful’. How Christians hold the warning and the promise, and a word to the afraid.
Hymenaeus and Philetus, who said the resurrection had already happened.
Correcting opponents gently, and never as a way to silence the harmed.
‘In the last days terrible times will come.’ No date, no modern group, and no verdict on women.
‘All who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.’ What it does and does not mean.
‘All Scripture is God-breathed.’ What all Christians confess, and inerrancy and infallibility, each fairly.
Paul facing death: the race finished and the crown laid up.
‘The Lord will repay him.’ Alexander, and a prayer for those who deserted Paul.
Elders: ‘the husband of but one wife’ and ‘children who are believers’. The readings, and character first.
‘Those of the circumcision.’ A dispute among believers, never a word against the Jewish people.
‘Cretans are always liars.’ A Cretan poet quoted against particular teachers, and never a licence for contempt of any people.
Older and younger women, and ‘submissive to their own husbands’. What all agree, both readings, and safety first.
Slaves and masters. Why Paul did not command the end of slavery, and the misuse of these verses.
‘Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.’ Christ's deity confessed.
‘Submit to rulers and authorities.’ Respect for every government, its limits, and no party lesson.
‘The washing of new birth.’ How churches read it of baptism, each fairly.
‘Reject a divisive man.’ Never a way to silence the harmed.
Onesimus. What the letter says about him, and what readers have inferred about how he came to Paul.
‘No longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.’ Why Paul did not command freedom, and the misuse of this letter.
‘Charge it to my account.’ Paul's pledge, and a picture of the gospel.
‘Even more than I ask.’ The main readings of what Paul hoped Philemon would do.
‘Your throne, O God.’ A psalm for a king applied to the Son, and what the church confesses.
‘Made perfect through suffering’ (2:10; 5:9). What it means, and what it does not mean.
Moses honoured, not belittled: faithful as a servant, Jesus as the Son.
‘A Sabbath rest remains.’ What the rest is, and how Christians differ on the Sabbath.
Loud cries and tears; ‘He learned obedience’. No suggestion that he was ever sinful.
‘It is impossible ... to be restored to repentance.’ The main readings, and a word to the afraid.
Melchizedek, ‘without father or mother’: what Genesis leaves unsaid.
‘Obsolete.’ A covenant arrangement, not a verdict on the Jewish people.
Covenant and will; ‘without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness’.
‘If we deliberately go on sinning.’ Not about a believer who struggles and repents.
Rahab the prostitute among the faithful, and saints who were not rescued.
The Lord's discipline: a father's training, never a cover for abuse or a verdict on the suffering.
Esau, who ‘could find no ground for repentance’.
‘Obey your leaders.’ Trust in accountable shepherds, never a shield for abuse.
‘Consider it pure joy’ in trials: not pretending, and not calling pain good.
‘God is tempting me.’ Testing and temptation, and why God is never the source of sin.
‘Pure and undefiled religion’: orphans and widows, and a bridled tongue.
Favouritism in the meeting, and God's choice of the poor.
‘Guilty of breaking all of it’, and ‘Mercy triumphs over judgment’.
‘Not by faith alone.’ James and Paul, and how the churches read 2:24.
‘We who teach will be judged more strictly.’
The tongue ‘set on fire by hell’: Gehenna and what it means.
‘You adulteresses’, friendship with the world, and the hard verse 4:5.
‘If the Lord is willing.’ Plans, and the shortness of life.
Woe to the rich who withheld wages: a prophet's word, not a party's.
Anointing the sick and ‘the prayer of faith’. Never a verdict that the sick lack faith.
Turning back the one who wanders, and covering ‘a multitude of sins’.
‘Chosen according to the foreknowledge of God’: Reformed and Arminian readings, and the comfort they share.
Trials that test faith like gold: not punishment, and not to be faced alone.
Redeemed by ‘the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish’.
Israel's titles given to the church. The views on Israel, and the misuse rejected.
‘Honor the king’: respect for rulers, and fear for God alone.
Slaves and masters. Never a defence of slavery, and a misuse named.
Wives and husbands: the main readings, and nothing that asks anyone to stay in danger.
‘Always be prepared to give a defense’, with gentleness and respect.
The spirits in prison: three readings, no side.
‘Baptism that now saves you’: what all share, and where churches differ.
The gospel ‘preached even to those who are now dead’.
The fiery trial, and judgment that begins ‘with the family of God’.
‘Cast all your anxiety on Him’: an invitation, never a rebuke.
‘The church in Babylon’ and Mark.
‘Our God and Savior Jesus Christ’: one of the plainest statements of Christ's deity.
‘Partakers of the divine nature’: theosis and the Western readings.
‘Make your calling and election sure’: Reformed and Arminian readings.
‘No prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation’: two readings.
‘The Master who bought them’: the false teachers, and the debate over verse 1.
The angels who sinned, Tartarus, and what 2 Peter shares with Jude.
Noah, Sodom and Lot: judgment and rescue.
‘Worse than at first’: can a believer fall away? The main readings.
‘A day is like a thousand years’: about patience, not a date.
‘Not wanting anyone to perish’: how the churches read it.
The day of the Lord: ‘laid bare’ or ‘burned up’, destroyed or renewed.
Paul's letters ‘hard to understand’, and counted with the Scriptures.
‘If we say we have no sin’: honesty about sin, and God's faithful forgiveness.
‘The whole world’: how the churches read the reach of Christ's sacrifice.
‘Many antichrists’: what John means, and why these notes name no one.
‘They went out from us’: those who left, and the readings on perseverance.
‘You do not need anyone to teach you’: the anointing, and the church's teachers.
‘He cannot go on sinning’: beside 1:8-10, the main readings.
‘Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer’.
‘God is greater than our hearts’: a word for the accusing conscience.
‘Test the spirits’: how to tell the Spirit of God from false teaching.
‘God is love’, and the God who judges.
The three witnesses, and the longer words found in later copies.
‘So that you may know’: assurance in 1 John.
‘A sin that leads to death’: the main readings, and what John does not say.
‘He is the true God and eternal life’.
‘The chosen lady and her children’: a church, or a woman who led one?
‘This is love, that we walk according to His commandments’.
‘The deceiver and the antichrist’: what the letter means, and why these notes name no one.
‘Anyone who runs ahead’: going beyond the teaching of Christ.
‘Do not receive him into your home’: what it meant, and what it does not mean.
‘That you may prosper and enjoy good health’: a friend's greeting, not a promise of wealth.
Hospitality to strangers: ‘fellow workers for the truth’.
‘Accepting nothing from the Gentiles’: why the workers took no support from unbelievers.
Diotrephes, ‘who loves to be first’: a leader who treats the church as his own.
‘The one who does evil has not seen God’.
‘Contend earnestly for the faith’: what Jude asks, and what he does not.
‘After Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt’: what the old copies show.
The angels who left their proper dwelling: the readings of Genesis 6.
Sodom and Gomorrah: how Christians read ‘strange flesh’.
Michael and the body of Moses: a tradition outside the Old Testament.
Enoch's prophecy and 1 Enoch: is quoting a book calling it Scripture?
‘Have mercy on those who doubt’.
‘Him who is able to keep you from stumbling’.
‘What must soon come to pass’ and ‘the time is near’: how the readings answer.
‘The seven Spirits before His throne’.
‘The angels of the seven churches’.
The Nicolaitans: what is known, and what is not.
‘The synagogue of Satan’: a local conflict, never a word about the Jewish people.
‘Where the throne of Satan sits’ at Pergamum.
‘That woman Jezebel’: what is known, and why it is no label for anyone today.
‘The synagogue of Satan’ again, at Philadelphia.
‘I will keep you from the hour of testing’: the rapture views.
‘Neither cold nor hot’.
‘I stand at the door and knock’, in its setting.
The number 666, and how readers have taken it.
The thousand years: the main views.
